guide.title: The Arrow and the Song — a guided reading and memorisation plan
guide.description: An unhurried reading of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s poem, with short passages, images, sound and gentle returns to the text.

metadata.chunkingStrategy: Passages within original stanzas; chunks of at most two lines. Read aloud and recall at your own pace, without scored exercises.

poem.title: The Arrow and the Song
poem.author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
poem.text:
I shot an arrow into the air,
It fell to earth, I knew not where;
For, so swiftly it flew, the sight
Could not follow it in its flight.

I breathed a song into the air,
It fell to earth, I knew not where;
For who has sight so keen and strong,
That it can follow the flight of song?

Long, long afterward, in an oak
I found the arrow, still unbroke;
And the song, from beginning to end,
I found again in the heart of a friend.

metadata.edition: Poetry Foundation public-domain transcription; three four-line stanzas.

sessions.title: Out of sight
sessions.focusSummary: Follow an arrow from release to disappearance.

pages.title: An invitation to read
pages.bodyMarkdown: Longfellow tells a small story about sending things beyond our sight. Read all twelve lines aloud before lingering with the opening stanza. Its paired rhymes will give the story a shape you can hear. You can take one stanza at a sitting, or stay with a favourite passage for longer.

pages.title: Stay with these lines
pages.bodyMarkdown: Read the passage aloud, following the sentence through the line endings. Pause over an image or sound that draws your attention.

pages.title: Out of sight
pages.bodyMarkdown: The first two lines tell us what happened; the next two explain why the speaker could not follow it. Let your voice move swiftly through the third line and into the fourth: the sentence crosses the line ending as the arrow crosses the sky. For memory, picture release, landing and the eye trying to keep up. The speaker admits a limit to what he knows.

pages.title: Let the words return
pages.bodyMarkdown: Hold the scene in mind and look away from the words. Try saying one or two lines, then return to the text wherever you need it. Join the passage together at a comfortable pace.

pages.title: A moment to linger
pages.prompt: How does the repeated uncertainty feel when you say the second line aloud?

pages.title: A place to pause
pages.bodyMarkdown: You can leave the passage here for a while. If an image or a sound stays with you, let it. Return whenever you would like to hear how the next lines continue the thought.

sessions.focusSummary: Hear the opening action return in another form.

pages.title: A different flight
pages.bodyMarkdown: The new stanza begins almost like the first, but a breath replaces the shot. Longfellow asks us to imagine a song travelling as an arrow travels. The second line returns word for word. Keep that familiar landing, then attend to the change from an explanation to a question. The rhyme between strong and song helps carry the question across its two lines.

sessions.title: Long afterward
sessions.focusSummary: Gather the two flights into the closing discovery.

pages.title: Long afterward
pages.bodyMarkdown: The doubled opening word slows the pace and lets time pass. First the arrow is found in an oak; then the song is found somewhere quite different. The stanza gives both journeys an ending without explaining how they got there. Say the whole poem and listen to the rhyme of end and friend. The last word makes the earlier solitary actions part of a relationship.

pages.prompt: What is the difference between finding an object and finding a song in another person?

pages.title: Keep the poem near
pages.bodyMarkdown: Let the poem rest for now. A phrase may return later, or you may want to read it aloud again with a different emphasis. Familiarity can grow through small, unhurried returns.
